newsitem.title: GHANA: Ghana's Rawlings on course for election victory.
newsitem.headline: Ghana's Rawlings on course for election victory.

text.p: Supporters of Ghana's populist president Jerry Rawlings turned out in festive mood after election results suggested he was on course for victory and a final four-year term.

Partial results from Saturday's national elections credited Rawlings with over 55 percent of the vote compared to under 42 percent for politician and businessman John Kufuor of the rejuvenated opposition's Great Alliance.

In the contest for the 200 seats in the West African gold and cocoa-producing nation's parliament, Rawlings's National Democratic Congress party also enjoyed a lead but the opposition alliance made significant advances.
"I am counting on at least 60 percent of the total votes to render a second round of no consequence," the 49-year-old Rawlings, who is half-Scottish, told Reuters on Sunday.

National Election Commission results, which will eventually be chalked onto a monster blackboard in Independence Square, covered only 64 of Ghana's 200 constituencies but unofficial results from 126 constituencies confirmed the trend.
"If this trend continues and I lose I will respect the traditional way," Kufuor told Reuters by telephone from his Accra home, adding that he would congratulate Rawlings.
Ghanaians voted peacefully on Saturday. Election Commission chairman Kwadwo Afari-Gyan estimated the turnout at 70 percent.

The Commonwealth Observer Group, among 100 foreign observers monitoring the poll, paid tribute to the organisation and conduct of the election. "We believe that the conditions existed for a free expression of will by the electors," it said.

Rawlings, who has been called everything from a dictator to a messiah, seized power as an air force flight-lieutenant in 1979, executing three former heads of state. He restored civilian rule but seized power again in 1981.

A former socialist firebrand, he embraced Western-style free-market economics -- winning plaudits from the International Monetary Fund and World Bank. He made the transition to elected president in disputed 1992 elections.

The main opposition learned the lesson of going into the 1992 elections in disarray and, against the odds, Kufuor's New Patriotic Party and the People's Convention Party formed a common front for this year's elections.
Kufuor, who celebrated his 58th birthday on Sunday, polled strongly in and around his stronghold of Kumasi, Ghana's second town and capital of the pre-colonial Ashanti empire.
Political pundits said he appeared to be taking more of the urban vote, with Rawlings winning more of the rural vote.
The third contender, surgeon Edward Mahama of the People's National Convention, trailed with just 2.58 percent of votes.
If no one wins outright, a run-off must be held in 21 days.
In the contest for parliament, which was being tallied separately, Rawlings's party had won 37 compared to 27 for the opposition alliance, according to the commission.
Latest unofficial results credited Rawlings's party with 54 seats and the opposition alliance with 33.
